question: A neonate born to an HBsAg-positive mother does not receive the birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine or HBIG. What is the approximate risk of this infant developing chronic HBV infection?

answers.text: 90% — neonatal immune tolerance permits persistent viraemia in the vast majority

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Neonates infected perinatally have ~90% risk of chronicity because their immature immune system develops tolerance to HBV rather than mounting an effective CTL response. This is why the birth-dose vaccine within 24 hours is critical to prevent vertical transmission.

answers.text: 50% — equal probability of clearance or chronicity at birth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 50% figure does not apply to any age group for HBV. Chronicity is age-dependent: ~90% in neonates, 30–50% in children aged 1–5 years, and only 5–10% in immunocompetent adults.

answers.text: 5–10% — the same rate as immunocompetent adults acquiring HBV

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 5–10% chronicity rate applies only to immunocompetent adults whose mature CTL response clears the virus in 90–95% of cases. Neonatal immune immaturity produces tolerance, not clearance.

answers.text: Less than 1% — passive maternal antibodies protect the neonate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Maternal antibodies do not prevent HBV chronicity in vertically infected neonates. In fact, the opposite is true — immune immaturity establishes tolerance, making perinatal infection the most dangerous acquisition route.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key concept: neonatal immune tolerance → 90% chronicity after perinatal HBV infection. This is why the Indian NIS mandates a birth-dose vaccine within 24 hours.
Age at infection determines chronicity: neonates 90%, children 30–50%, adults 5–10%. Birth-dose vaccine prevents this outcome.
